The Moor frog (Rana arvalis) exhibits life-history traits that are broadly comparable to those of its congener Rana temporaria, though subtle differences in body size and developmental timing are increasingly recognized from field studies. Emerging from hibernation in early spring, adults migrate to shallow, fish-free breeding ponds where amplexus and external fertilisation occur. The gelatinous egg masses, which contain between 500 and 3000 eggs [N_R_i = contain between 500 and 3000 eggs] per single clutch deposited each year [F_R_i = single clutch deposited each year], are laid in the warmest, sun-exposed microhabitats of the pond. This single annual reproductive event is influenced by water temperature, and under controlled conditions set at 10 °C [T = 10 °C], the incubation period from oviposition to hatching averages approximately 35 days [ab = approximately 35 days], a developmental rate that aligns well with that documented in Rana temporaria at a similar thermal regime. The tiny larvae that emerge weigh approximately 0.05 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.05 grams] at birth, a value estimated from comparable bufonid data, marking the onset of the exotrophic, aquatic tadpole stage.

During the subsequent larval period, tadpoles of Rana arvalis progress through a series of Gosner stages as they feed actively on algae and detritus, fueling a rapid increase in body mass. The duration of this free-swimming, gill-breathing phase is strongly temperature-dependent. In a laboratory study, when tadpoles were reared at a constant 18 °C [T = 18 °C], the time from hatching to the onset of metamorphic climax was recorded as approximately 46 days after hatching . This duration, which represents the time since birth at metamorphosis, falls within the range reported for Rana temporaria under similar thermal conditions and highlights the role of accumulated thermal units in mediating larval growth and development before the initiation of limb bud growth and tail resorption. Following metamorphosis, the recently metamorphosed juvenile froglets, which are commonly referred to as froglets, measure about 1.5 centimeters  in body length. This body length at the larval-juvenile transition marks a critical allometric shift as the animal begins its largely terrestrial existence.

After the terrestrial juvenile phase, the growing froglets enter a period of sexual maturation that culminates in the ability to reproduce. For the Moor frog, the age at which these immature post-metamorphic individuals attain puberty is estimated at approximately 2 years following metamorphosis [tp = approximately 2 years following metamorphosis] when maintained at 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. This value, which is derived from the same thermal regime used for the larval measurements, suggests that individuals generally do not breed until at least their second or third year of life, a pattern consistent with that of many temperate ranid frogs. During this protracted juvenile period, the frogs continue to increase in both length and mass, feeding on terrestrial invertebrates to accumulate the energy reserves necessary for overwintering and eventual gonad maturation.

Adult Rana arvalis reach a maximum snout-to-vent length that is well documented in the herpetological literature. The ultimate body length for the species, meaning the largest size attained by fully grown individuals, is approximately 7 centimeters [Li = approximately 7 centimeters]. Associated with this ceiling on skeletal growth is a corresponding ultimate wet weight of roughly 31 grams [Wwi = roughly 31 grams], a value that represents the maximum adult body mass when individuals reach that length. This body mass is relatively modest compared to some other European ranids, and it reflects the Moor frog's adaptation to cooler, more ephemeral breeding habitats. The longevity of this species is also constrained; maximum lifespan in the wild has been recorded at up to 11 years [am = up to 11 years] when measured at 18 °C [T = 18 °C], a figure that emerged from a long-term mark-recapture study conducted under field conditions.

Comparative physiological data allow for contextualizing the life history of Rana arvalis within the broader framework of European amphibian ecology. The maximum reproductive rate involves a single clutch produced each year [F_R_i = a single clutch produced each year], containing 500 to 3000 eggs [N_R_i = containing 500 to 3000 eggs], a strategy that underscores the reliance on a sizable annual investment rather than multiple smaller clutches. Interestingly, while the lifespan itself is measured at 18 °C [T = 18 °C], the age at hatching is typically recorded at a cooler incubation temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], reflecting the cold-water conditions of early spring breeding ponds. Together, these traits illustrate a life history strategy finely tuned to the short, cold growing seasons of northern and central European wetlands.
